items.stem: Which of the following best describes "probe"?
options: A follow-up question used to obtain more detail or clarification
Using different methods (e.g. experiment and interview) to study the same question
A method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) in qualitative data (Braun and Clarke, 2006)
A qualitative analysis in which categories are derived from the data rather than decided in advance
items.answer: A follow-up question used to obtain more detail or clarification
items.markingKey: A. "probe" is a follow-up question used to obtain more detail or clarification.

items.stem: Distinguish between an unstructured interview and a semi-structured interview.
items.answer: A semi-structured interview follows an interview schedule but allows probes; an unstructured interview has no fixed schedule and is led more by the interviewee.
items.markingKey: A semi-structured interview follows an interview schedule but allows probes; an unstructured interview has no fixed schedule and is led more by the interviewee. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why rapport is important in interviews.
items.answer: When interviewees trust the interviewer, they are more willing to share honest, detailed and sensitive information, increasing the credibility of the data.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: When interviewees trust the interviewer, they are more willing to share honest, detailed and sensitive information, increasing the credibility of the data. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe a telephone survey of voters and explain what it reveals about structured interviews.
items.answer: A polling company in Mexico City phones 1,000 adults and reads the same ten questions with fixed answer options to each. Identical questions and options produce comparable, quantifiable data from a large sample, but answers lack depth
items.markingKey: Context (A polling company in Mexico City phones 1,000 adults and reads the same ten questions with fixed answer options to each.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: identical questions and options produce comparable, quantifiable data from a large sample, but answers lack depth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structured interviews.

items.stem: A researcher studies the life histories of elderly migrants who arrived in the UK in the 1950s. Recommend an interview format and justify your choice, including one limitation of that format.
items.answer: Unstructured interview - life-history research follows the participant's narrative rather than a fixed schedule.
items.markingKey: 1 mark format (unstructured interview); 2 marks justification (life-history research follows the participant's narrative rather than a fixed schedule); 1 mark relevant limitation (structured: little depth; semi/unstructured: harder to compare, interviewer effects, time-consuming analysis).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Semi-structured interviews are the best type of interview for psychological research."
items.answer: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: balance between comparability and depth; allow probing of meanings. Arguments against: structured interviews better for comparison and reliability; unstructured interviews allow more participant-led data; interviewer effects and time-consuming analysis. Supported judgement: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "structured interview".
items.answer: An interview using fixed questions in a fixed order for every participant
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an interview using fixed questions in a fixed order for every participant. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Unstructured interviews are unscientific because each one is different." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Unstructured interviews aim for depth and meaning, not comparability; their rigour comes from reflexivity, careful analysis and credibility checks.
items.markingKey: Unstructured interviews aim for depth and meaning, not comparability; their rigour comes from reflexivity, careful analysis and credibility checks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain two things an interviewer should do at the start of an interview to build rapport.
items.answer: Explain the purpose, confidentiality and right to withdraw in plain language; start with easy, non-threatening questions; choose a comfortable, private setting; use open body language and active listening.
items.markingKey: Explain the purpose, confidentiality and right to withdraw in plain language; start with easy, non-threatening questions; choose a comfortable, private setting; use open body language and active listening.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that semi-structured interviews are the best type of interview for psychological research.
items.answer: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question.
items.markingKey: For: balance between comparability and depth; allow probing of meanings. Against: structured interviews better for comparison and reliability; unstructured interviews allow more participant-led data; interviewer effects and time-consuming analysis. Supported conclusion: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question. Markbands (15), applied holistically: 13-15 - the response is focused on the command term and the question throughout; knowledge and understanding of the relevant concepts, theories and studies is accurate and detailed; research is clearly explained and explicitly linked to the argument; critical thinking is well developed (methodological, ethical and cultural evaluation, alternative explanations, the six concepts where relevant) and leads to a reasoned conclusion. 10-12 - focused; accurate knowledge; relevant research mostly linked to the question; evaluation present but uneven. 7-9 - partly focused; some accurate knowledge; research described more than used; evaluation limited or generic. 4-6 - limited focus; knowledge partly accurate; research only named or poorly linked; little evaluation. 1-3 - very limited relevant knowledge, no evaluation. 0 - does not reach band 1.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A qualitative analysis in which categories are derived from the data rather than decided in advance"?
items.answer: inductive content analysis
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of inductive content analysis.

items.stem: Explain why inductive analysis is useful in interview research.
items.answer: It allows themes to emerge from participants' own words rather than imposing the researcher's categories, so unexpected issues can be found and the findings reflect participants' perspectives.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It allows themes to emerge from participants' own words rather than imposing the researcher's categories, so unexpected issues can be found and the findings reflect participants' perspectives. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A theme is just a topic that appears often in the data." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A theme captures a pattern of meaning relevant to the research question; frequency alone does not make something a theme.
items.markingKey: A theme captures a pattern of meaning relevant to the research question; frequency alone does not make something a theme. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the interview extract.

"I check my phone the second I wake up. If I have no messages I feel kind of invisible... but when I leave it in the kitchen I actually read more."

Identify three initial codes from this extract using inductive analysis.
items.answer: Possible codes: need for social validation; habitual phone checking; benefits of phone separation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each relevant code grounded in the extract (accept equivalent labels): need for social validation; habitual phone checking; benefits of phone separation. Codes that are not supported by the text score 0.

items.stem: Read this extract and identify two initial codes: "When I moved to Toronto I stopped speaking up in class... in Seoul you wait until the teacher asks you... now I feel stupid when others just talk."
items.answer: Codes: "cultural norms about classroom participation" (waiting to be asked); "loss of confidence/self-esteem" ("feel stupid"); possibly "comparison with peers".
items.markingKey: Codes: "cultural norms about classroom participation" (waiting to be asked); "loss of confidence/self-esteem" ("feel stupid"); possibly "comparison with peers".

items.stem: Using a transcript about exam stress as an example, explain thematic analysis.
items.answer: Interviewee: "My parents never say it, but I know they expect top grades... I study until 2 a.m. and then I can't sleep... my friends are the only ones who get it." Codes such as "implicit parental expectations", "late-night studying", "sleep problems" and "peer support" could be grouped into themes like "pressure" and "coping through peers"
items.markingKey: Context (Interviewee: "My parents never say it, but I know they expect top grades... I study until 2 a.m. and then I can't sleep... my friends are the only ones who get it.") – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: codes such as "implicit parental expectations", "late-night studying", "sleep problems" and "peer support" could be grouped into themes like "pressure" and "coping through peers" – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thematic analysis.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Thematic analysis produces subjective findings."
items.answer: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: researcher interprets data; different researchers may find different themes. Arguments against: systematic phases (Braun and Clarke, 2006); credibility checks (member checking, triangulation); reflexivity makes interpretation transparent. Supported judgement: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy.

items.stem: Critically assess the view that thematic analysis produces subjective findings. Consider at least one methodological and one ethical or cultural issue.
items.answer: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy.
items.markingKey: For: researcher interprets data; different researchers may find different themes. Against: systematic phases (Braun and Clarke, 2006); credibility checks (member checking, triangulation); reflexivity makes interpretation transparent. Supported conclusion: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: Explain why two researchers might code the same transcript independently.
items.answer: Comparing codes (researcher triangulation) checks whether interpretations are consistent, reduces individual bias and increases credibility.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Comparing codes (researcher triangulation) checks whether interpretations are consistent, reduces individual bias and increases credibility. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a code and a theme.
items.answer: A code labels a single meaningful segment of data (e.g. "fear of failure"); a theme is a broader pattern that groups related codes across the data (e.g. "pressure to perform").
items.markingKey: A code labels a single meaningful segment of data (e.g. "fear of failure"); a theme is a broader pattern that groups related codes across the data (e.g. "pressure to perform"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to a transcript about exam stress, explain how it illustrates thematic analysis.
items.answer: Interviewee: "My parents never say it, but I know they expect top grades... I study until 2 a.m. and then I can't sleep... my friends are the only ones who get it." Codes such as "implicit parental expectations", "late-night studying", "sleep problems" and "peer support" could be grouped into themes like "pressure" and "coping through peers"
items.markingKey: Context (Interviewee: "My parents never say it, but I know they expect top grades... I study until 2 a.m. and then I can't sleep... my friends are the only ones who get it.") – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: codes such as "implicit parental expectations", "late-night studying", "sleep problems" and "peer support" could be grouped into themes like "pressure" and "coping through peers" – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thematic analysis.

items.stem:
Read the interview extract.

"In my old school in Lagos the teacher explained, then we copied. Here they ask our opinion all the time. At first I hated it, now I like debating."

Identify a possible theme related to culture and learning, support it with evidence from the extract, and explain one way the researcher could check the credibility of this interpretation.
items.answer: Theme related to culture and learning, built from codes such as contrasting teaching styles; initial discomfort with new norms; adaptation over time. Credibility: member checking or a second coder (researcher triangulation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark theme; 2 marks supporting quotations/codes (contrasting teaching styles; initial discomfort with new norms; adaptation over time); 2 marks credibility check explained (member checking, researcher triangulation, reflexivity, audit trail).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "credibility".
items.answer: The extent to which qualitative findings accurately represent participants' experiences
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the extent to which qualitative findings accurately represent participants' experiences. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between transferability and credibility.
items.answer: Credibility concerns whether findings accurately represent the participants' experiences; transferability concerns whether they can apply to other settings.
items.markingKey: Credibility concerns whether findings accurately represent the participants' experiences; transferability concerns whether they can apply to other settings. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Interview findings cannot be useful because the samples are small." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Small purposive samples are appropriate for depth; findings can be credible and transferable to similar contexts, and can generate hypotheses for larger studies.
items.markingKey: Small purposive samples are appropriate for depth; findings can be credible and transferable to similar contexts, and can generate hypotheses for larger studies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student wants to interview a friend about her eating disorder for a class practical. Identify the main ethical issue and explain how it should be addressed.
items.answer: Issue: protection from harm and the sensitivity of the topic (also the dual relationship of friend and researcher). Response: choose a less sensitive topic; if any, ensure support is available, the right to withdraw is clear and the friend is not pressured.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: issue (protection from harm and the sensitivity of the topic (also the dual relationship of friend and researcher)). 1-2 marks: explanation of why it matters in this context. 1 mark: appropriate action (choose a less sensitive topic; if any, ensure support is available, the right to withdraw is clear and the friend is not pressured).

items.stem: A student interviewed one classmate about exam anxiety. Suggest two ways she could increase the credibility of her findings and one way she could support transferability.
items.answer: Credibility: member checking, a second coder, reflexive notes on her relationship with the classmate. Transferability: thick description of the participant, school context and timing.
items.markingKey: Credibility: member checking, a second coder, reflexive notes on her relationship with the classmate. Transferability: thick description of the participant, school context and timing.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Interview research can be as credible as experimental research."
items.answer: Interviews can be highly credible for questions about experience and meaning, although they cannot answer causal questions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: credibility checks and triangulation; rich, valid data about meaning. Arguments against: researcher bias and interviewer effects; small samples; no causal conclusions. Supported judgement: Interviews can be highly credible for questions about experience and meaning, although they cannot answer causal questions.

items.stem: Which ethical issue is particularly important when quoting interviewees in a report?
options: Confidentiality - quotations must not identify participants
items.answer: Confidentiality - quotations must not identify participants
items.markingKey: A. Use pseudonyms and remove identifying details.

items.stem: With reference to two coders who disagree, explain how it illustrates researcher triangulation.
items.answer: Two students code the same interview transcript independently; one finds a theme of "family pressure", the other "self-imposed pressure". Discussing disagreements and returning to the data refines the themes and reduces individual bias, increasing credibility
items.markingKey: Context (Two students code the same interview transcript independently; one finds a theme of "family pressure", the other "self-imposed pressure".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: discussing disagreements and returning to the data refines the themes and reduces individual bias, increasing credibility – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to researcher triangulation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Interview findings cannot be useful because the samples are small." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Small purposive samples are appropriate for depth; findings can be credible and transferable to similar contexts, and can generate hypotheses for larger studies.
items.markingKey: Small purposive samples are appropriate for depth; findings can be credible and transferable to similar contexts, and can generate hypotheses for larger studies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the four class practicals is best for establishing cause and effect?
items.answer: The experiment
items.markingKey: The experiment. Only the experiment manipulates an IV with controls.

items.stem: Explain why combining an experiment with interviews could strengthen a study.
items.answer: The experiment shows whether the IV causes a change in the DV; interviews explain how participants experienced the conditions and why, revealing mechanisms and demand characteristics.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The experiment shows whether the IV causes a change in the DV; interviews explain how participants experienced the conditions and why, revealing mechanisms and demand characteristics. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Quantitative methods are always more scientific than qualitative methods." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Both can be rigorous; the appropriate method depends on the research question, and qualitative research has its own standards (credibility, transferability, reflexivity).
items.markingKey: Both can be rigorous; the appropriate method depends on the research question, and qualitative research has its own standards (credibility, transferability, reflexivity). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe a study of phone use in class and explain what it reveals about comparing methods.
items.answer: Researchers in Seoul surveyed 400 students about phone use in lessons, observed 20 lessons and interviewed 10 students; students reported less use than was observed. Triangulation reveals social desirability bias in the survey; observation gives behavioural data and interviews explain motives
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers in Seoul surveyed 400 students about phone use in lessons, observed 20 lessons and interviewed 10 students; students reported less use than was observed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: triangulation reveals social desirability bias in the survey; observation gives behavioural data and interviews explain motives – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparing methods.

items.stem: A study in Vienna compares the number of helping acts performed by children who watched a prosocial cartoon with those who watched a neutral cartoon. Explain why this study can or cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.
items.answer: Because type of cartoon (prosocial vs neutral) is manipulated by the researcher and other variables are controlled, a causal claim about its effect on number of times the child helped pick up dropped pencils in a 5-minute test is possible - provided extraneous variables such as those noted are controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: whether the IV is manipulated/randomly allocated; 1 mark: role of controls/confounds; 1 mark: conclusion about causality applied to this study.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "No single research method can fully explain behaviour."
items.answer: Combining methods usually gives a fuller explanation, although a single well-chosen method can answer a focused question.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each method has limitations (causality vs ecological validity vs meaning); triangulation increases credibility. Arguments against: some questions are best answered by one method; mixed methods are costly and complex. Supported judgement: Combining methods usually gives a fuller explanation, although a single well-chosen method can answer a focused question.

items.stem: Briefly explain why observations and surveys may give different results about the same behaviour.
items.answer: Surveys measure what people say they do (subject to social desirability and memory errors); observations record what people actually do, so the two can diverge.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Surveys measure what people say they do (subject to social desirability and memory errors); observations record what people actually do, so the two can diverge. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A researcher wants to study whether a mindfulness programme reduces stress in students. Explain how two different class-practical methods could be combined.
items.answer: Experiment (randomly allocate to programme or waiting list; measure PSS scores) plus semi-structured interviews with participants about how they used the techniques - giving causal evidence and insight into mechanisms.
items.markingKey: Experiment (randomly allocate to programme or waiting list; measure PSS scores) plus semi-structured interviews with participants about how they used the techniques - giving causal evidence and insight into mechanisms.

items.stem: In Braun and Clarke's (2006) thematic analysis, what is the first phase?
items.answer: Familiarising yourself with the data
items.markingKey: D. The six phases: familiarisation, initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming, writing up.

items.stem: Which type of interview gives the most comparable data between participants?
items.answer: Structured
items.markingKey: C. Fixed questions in a fixed order make answers easy to compare.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The extent to which qualitative findings accurately represent participants' experiences"?

items.stem: Distinguish between the observation practical and the survey practical.
items.answer: A survey gathers self-reported attitudes or behaviour from many people quickly; an observation records actual behaviour directly but takes longer and cannot access thoughts.
items.markingKey: A survey gathers self-reported attitudes or behaviour from many people quickly; an observation records actual behaviour directly but takes longer and cannot access thoughts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between inductive analysis and deductive analysis.
items.answer: Inductive analysis develops categories from the data; deductive analysis applies categories derived from existing theory.
items.markingKey: Inductive analysis develops categories from the data; deductive analysis applies categories derived from existing theory. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why interviews raise particular ethical concerns.
items.answer: They often involve personal, sensitive topics, recordings and identifiable quotations, so informed consent, confidentiality, the right to withdraw (including data) and protection from distress are crucial.

items.stem: An interviewer's first question is "Don't you think the school is too strict?" Explain the problem and rewrite the question.
items.answer: It is a leading question that suggests the answer; rewrite as "How would you describe the school's rules?" with probes such as "Can you tell me more about that?"

items.stem: Explain how a researcher could write a reflexive statement for an interview study on discrimination experienced by Muslim students in France.
items.answer: State her own identity and beliefs (e.g. religion, nationality), relationship to participants, and how these may have shaped questions, rapport and interpretation; explain steps taken to limit bias (second coder, member checks).
items.markingKey: State her own identity and beliefs (e.g. religion, nationality), relationship to participants, and how these may have shaped questions, rapport and interpretation; explain steps taken to limit bias (second coder, member checks).

items.stem: Describe the steps a student should take to turn interview transcripts into themes.
items.answer: Transcribe verbatim; read and re-read; generate initial codes line by line; collate codes into candidate themes; review themes against the data; define and name themes; select illustrative quotes; ideally a second coder checks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "transcript"?
options: A method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) in qualitative data (Braun and Clarke, 2006)
The influence of the interviewer's characteristics or behaviour on the interviewee's answers
The qualitative equivalent of reliability: the extent to which the research process is consistent and documented
A written, word-for-word record of an interview
items.answer: A written, word-for-word record of an interview
items.markingKey: D. "transcript" is a written, word-for-word record of an interview.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A follow-up question used to obtain more detail or clarification"?
items.answer: probe
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of probe.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dependability"?
options: The qualitative equivalent of reliability: the extent to which the research process is consistent and documented
Using different methods (e.g. experiment and interview) to study the same question
An interview using fixed questions in a fixed order for every participant
A detailed description of the context, participants and process of a study that allows readers to judge transferability
items.answer: The qualitative equivalent of reliability: the extent to which the research process is consistent and documented
items.markingKey: A. "dependability" is the qualitative equivalent of reliability: the extent to which the research process is consistent and documented.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the experiment practical and the interview practical.
items.answer: The experiment manipulates an IV to test causal hypotheses with quantitative data; the interview explores meanings and experiences with qualitative data.
items.markingKey: The experiment manipulates an IV to test causal hypotheses with quantitative data; the interview explores meanings and experiences with qualitative data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A theme is just a topic that appears often in the data." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A theme captures a pattern of meaning relevant to the research question; frequency alone does not make something a theme.
items.markingKey: A theme captures a pattern of meaning relevant to the research question; frequency alone does not make something a theme. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Unstructured interviews are unscientific because each one is different." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Unstructured interviews aim for depth and meaning, not comparability; their rigour comes from reflexivity, careful analysis and credibility checks.
items.markingKey: Unstructured interviews aim for depth and meaning, not comparability; their rigour comes from reflexivity, careful analysis and credibility checks. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between transferability and credibility.
items.answer: Credibility concerns whether findings accurately represent the participants' experiences; transferability concerns whether they can apply to other settings.
items.markingKey: Credibility concerns whether findings accurately represent the participants' experiences; transferability concerns whether they can apply to other settings. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the interview practical and the experiment practical.
items.answer: The experiment manipulates an IV to test causal hypotheses with quantitative data; the interview explores meanings and experiences with qualitative data.
items.markingKey: The experiment manipulates an IV to test causal hypotheses with quantitative data; the interview explores meanings and experiences with qualitative data. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a theme and a code.
items.answer: A code labels a single meaningful segment of data (e.g. "fear of failure"); a theme is a broader pattern that groups related codes across the data (e.g. "pressure to perform").
items.markingKey: A code labels a single meaningful segment of data (e.g. "fear of failure"); a theme is a broader pattern that groups related codes across the data (e.g. "pressure to perform"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to a telephone survey of voters, explain how it illustrates structured interviews.
items.answer: A polling company in Mexico City phones 1,000 adults and reads the same ten questions with fixed answer options to each. Identical questions and options produce comparable, quantifiable data from a large sample, but answers lack depth
items.markingKey: Context (A polling company in Mexico City phones 1,000 adults and reads the same ten questions with fixed answer options to each.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: identical questions and options produce comparable, quantifiable data from a large sample, but answers lack depth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to structured interviews.

items.stem: A researcher plans to publish long quotations from interviews with teachers at a small rural school. Identify the main ethical issue and explain how it should be addressed.
items.answer: Issue: confidentiality - quotations and context may identify individuals. Response: use pseudonyms, remove identifying details, ask participants to approve quotations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality - quotations and context may identify individuals). 1-2 marks: explanation of why it matters in this context. 1 mark: appropriate action (use pseudonyms, remove identifying details, ask participants to approve quotations).

items.stem: In Seoul, 50 adolescents and 50 adults play a computer driving game, and the number of risky decisions is recorded with or without peers watching. Explain why this study can or cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.
items.answer: Because age group and peer presence is not randomly assigned (mixed design: age is a quasi-IV (independent groups); peer presence could be repeated measures), confounding participant variables mean causality is limited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: whether the IV is manipulated/randomly allocated; 1 mark: role of controls/confounds; 1 mark: conclusion about causality applied to this study.

items.stem:
Read the interview extract.

"After my grandmother died I couldn't concentrate. My teacher let me hand in work late, and my friends walked home with me every day."

Identify three initial codes from this extract using inductive analysis.
items.answer: Possible codes: grief affecting concentration; flexible support from school; peer social support.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each relevant code grounded in the extract (accept equivalent labels): grief affecting concentration; flexible support from school; peer social support. Codes that are not supported by the text score 0.

items.stem: Write three questions for a semi-structured interview schedule on adolescents' experiences of moving to a new country, including one probe.
items.answer: E.g. "Can you tell me about your first weeks at your new school?" "What has helped you feel at home?" "What has been most difficult?" Probe: "Can you give me an example of that?"
items.markingKey: E.g. "Can you tell me about your first weeks at your new school?" "What has helped you feel at home?" "What has been most difficult?" Probe: "Can you give me an example of that?"

items.stem: Using a study of rural teachers with thick description as an example, explain transferability.
items.answer: A report on interviews with teachers in rural Kenya gives detailed information about class sizes, distances travelled and community expectations. Thick description lets readers judge whether the findings may apply to teachers in similar rural contexts elsewhere
items.markingKey: Context (A report on interviews with teachers in rural Kenya gives detailed information about class sizes, distances travelled and community expectations.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: thick description lets readers judge whether the findings may apply to teachers in similar rural contexts elsewhere – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transferability.

items.stem: Using a study of phone use in class as an example, explain comparing methods.
items.answer: Researchers in Seoul surveyed 400 students about phone use in lessons, observed 20 lessons and interviewed 10 students; students reported less use than was observed. Triangulation reveals social desirability bias in the survey; observation gives behavioural data and interviews explain motives
items.markingKey: Context (Researchers in Seoul surveyed 400 students about phone use in lessons, observed 20 lessons and interviewed 10 students; students reported less use than was observed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: triangulation reveals social desirability bias in the survey; observation gives behavioural data and interviews explain motives – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparing methods.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Thematic analysis produces subjective findings."
items.answer: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: researcher interprets data; different researchers may find different themes. Arguments against: systematic phases (Braun and Clarke, 2006); credibility checks (member checking, triangulation); reflexivity makes interpretation transparent. Supported judgement: Thematic analysis is interpretive, but systematic procedures and credibility checks make findings trustworthy.

items.stem: "Semi-structured interviews are the best type of interview for psychological research." Evaluate this claim with reference to research.
items.answer: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question.
items.markingKey: For: balance between comparability and depth; allow probing of meanings. Against: structured interviews better for comparison and reliability; unstructured interviews allow more participant-led data; interviewer effects and time-consuming analysis. Supported conclusion: Semi-structured interviews are often the best compromise, but the choice depends on the research question. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: "Interview research can be as credible as experimental research." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Interviews can be highly credible for questions about experience and meaning, although they cannot answer causal questions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: credibility checks and triangulation; rich, valid data about meaning. Arguments against: researcher bias and interviewer effects; small samples; no causal conclusions. Supported judgement: Interviews can be highly credible for questions about experience and meaning, although they cannot answer causal questions.
